The pad now comes from the prefix size. fbs_lite rootTable also accepts a vtable placed after the table (negative soffset), bounds-checked exactly as the verifier does.
- G2: record batches and dictionary batches with body_length 0 (zero rows, all null) decode with an empty body; every buffer descriptor is still checked against the body length.
- G3: dictionary ids nested inside another dictionary's value type are found. A dictionary whose value type contains its own id is rejected: each replacement would chain to the previous one and recursion would grow with the stream.
- G4: SharedBuffer.typedSlice returns an empty slice for a zero-length buffer instead of MisalignedPointer (unions, run-end-encoded, list views). Empty binary/list arrays that old writers send without an offsets buffer get a single 0 offset at the IPC boundary, so validateLayout and the kernels keep assuming length + 1 offsets.
Six tests on five arrow-testing fixtures (Apache-2.0, NOTICE in src/ipc/testdata). 375 tests and the fuzz corpus pass on Zig 0.16 and 0.17; a 120 s ReleaseSafe campaign on ipc-stream and ipc-file found nothing; ipc_roundtrip is unchanged." -m "Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com>" && git log --oneline -1 && git status --short | wc -l

content.text:
The compat work is on master and pushed as e93f5c3, two commits.

**The four gaps, and what they really were.** The agent's investigation overturned the earlier diagnosis of the first one. Arrow 0.14.1 streams were not failing on vtable placement. They use a 4-byte length prefix, and the reader skipped padding computed for the 8-byte prefix, so it ate four bytes of the next message and parsed garbage. The pad is now derived from the prefix size. The other three were as diagnosed: batches with an empty body are now decoded with an empty buffer and every descriptor still checked against it, dictionary lookup recurses into dictionary value types, and zero-length buffers no longer fail as misaligned. Empty binary and list arrays that old writers send with no offsets buffer get a single zero offset at the IPC boundary, so the kernels keep their length-plus-one invariant and no validator was loosened.

**One hardening came with it.** A dictionary whose value type contains its own id is now rejected. Each replacement batch would have chained to the previous dictionary, and recursion would have grown with the stream length.

**Replay of arrow-testing integration fixtures:**

| set | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| stream, decoded of 91 | 43 | 67 |
| file, decoded of 91 | 59 | 67 |

The remaining 24 of each are unsigned dictionary indices and big-endian files, both policy choices left alone.

**The Docker campaign earned its place immediately.** Run on the compat commit, it found two things on Linux that the Windows checks had passed. The coverage-guided fuzzer hit an out-of-bounds read in the C ABI importer: a null offsets pointer imports as an empty buffer, and the zero-length change had turned a masked misalignment error into a real unchecked index. Offsets now must hold length plus one entries or the import fails. The mutation run found that slicing a valid run-end-encoded array to length zero failed validateFull, because the validator demanded zero run ends at zero length, stricter than Arrow. Both are fixed with regression seeds, and the rerun was clean: 6.4 million mutation executions and 14.6k coverage-guided runs, no findings. 375 tests pass on both compilers.

content.text:
Yes, and the biggest one is the same shape as the last three rounds: a fast path exists for a few layouts and everything else falls through to a per-row loop.

**Worth doing, ranked by gain:**

1. **Take and filter on nested and encoded types.** The direct kernels cover fixed-width, bool, string, binary, list and large list. Struct, dictionary, fixed-size list, union, map, list views, run-end-encoded and extension types fall through to a path that builds a one-row array per index and concatenates them. The planner measured struct take at about 3 microseconds per row, against 2 nanoseconds for int32. Struct is a recursion into the child kernels plus one validity gather. Dictionary is a take on the indices alone with the dictionary shared. Fixed-size list is an index expansion. Those three cover nearly all real data and would be a 500 to 1000 times gain on the types they hit.

2. **Chunked take and filter.** Chunked inputs use the same per-row element path regardless of type. Mapping indices to chunk and local offset, then running the per-chunk kernels, puts chunked within a small factor of flat.

3. **Nested concat.** List and struct concat still merge pairwise, so many parts cost O(n log n) copies. The N-ary path from round two extends naturally: rebase offsets and concat the child once, or concat each struct child once.

**Measured and at the floor, not worth touching:**

- IPC write is at memcpy speed for the body. The gap to Arrow C++ is in the measurement harness, not the copy.
- Compressed IPC sits on libzstd itself. The only lever left is compressing the buffers of one batch on separate threads, a wall-clock gain rather than a CPU one.
- The flat builders, the flat kernels, concat of flat types, and both IPC read paths are at or ahead of arrow-rs.
- Struct builder measures 3.5 ns per row and the record batch builder 5. Fine for what they do.

**Not measured, so unknown:** dictionary encoding and unification, and the cost of UTF-8 validation inside validateFull on large string columns. Those would need a benchmark before anyone touches them.

Items one through three are what the Phase 2 card describes. The box above asks whether to do them here now.

Repo worktree (clean, HEAD 362ecf1; must build on Zig 0.16 and 0.17): C:\Users\cable\Documents\dev\zarrow\.claude\worktrees\zig-0-17-migration-branch-f92e21. Do NOT edit that worktree. ## Goal: remove the per-row fallbacks
Rounds 1-3 (see git log, src/compute/datum_permutation.zig, src/concat_array_refs.zig) gave direct kernels for take/filter on fixed-width, bool, string/binary (i32/i64) and list/large_list, and an N-ary concat for flat layouts. Everything else still goes through a per-row path:
- datumTakeArrayLikeNullable falls back to `accessors.datumElementArrayAt` + `buildNullLikeArray` per index, then concat (datum_permutation.zig ~line 520). Measured: struct take ~3092 ns/row vs 1.9 for int32. Affected layouts: struct, dictionary, fixed_size_list, sparse/dense union, map, list_view/large_list_view, run_end_encoded, extension (storage type), null type, fixed_size_binary (check whether takeFixedWidthArray already covers it), decimal/interval widths.
- datumTakeChunkedNullable (and the chunked predicate/filter paths around lines 700-760) use the same per-row element path for chunked datums regardless of type.
- concatArrayRefs: nested layouts (list, large_list, struct, fixed_size_list, map, unions, dictionary, extension) still use the pairwise mergePairs (O(n log n) copies with many parts).

Targets (ns/row, 200k rows x 80 iters shapes like benchmarks/take_benchmark.zig): struct take <30 (ideally <10: int32 child + string child), dictionary take <5 (indices-only), fixed_size_list take <10, chunked take/filter within 2x of flat, list and struct N-ary concat with 12,500 parts of 16 rows <10 (int32 list / struct{int32,string}). Numbers must be measured with new benchmarks you add: benchmarks/take_nested_benchmark.zig (struct, dictionary, fixed_size_list, and a chunked int32 take), benchmarks/concat_nested_benchmark.zig (list<int32> and struct{int32,string} with 16-row parts), registered the same way as take_benchmark.zig/concat_benchmark.zig in build.zig, tools/benchmark_ci_check.py, tools/test_benchmark_ci_check.py and tools/benchmark_ci_thresholds.json (follow the existing entries; CSV `ci` mode must work). Report before/after for each, alternating base and new runs (the planner of round 3 left $S\ab.sh; adapt or write your own), plus the existing take/filter/concat benchmarks to prove no regression.

## Design guidance (verify against the code, do not assume)
- Struct take: validity = gatherBits over the struct's own bitmap (reuse gatherBits/checkIndices/validityBytes), children = recurse datumTakeArrayLikeNullable with the SAME indices (children are row-aligned when child.length == parent.length; a child in parent coordinates (offset-driven) must be handled: look at how array_ref.zig slice and array_data.zig childCoversRange treat the two coordinate spaces, and take child rows at parent offset + idx). Null struct rows still take a child row (arrow-rs does the same) OR emit null child rows; pick the one that keeps child validity consistent and say which.
- Dictionary take: take the indices array with the fixed-width kernel, keep the dictionary ArrayRef retained. Null indices stay null.
- Fixed-size list: validity gather + child take with expanded indices (idx*list_size + k), recursing into the kernels, like takeListArray does for list.
- Extension: take the storage layout and re-wrap with the extension type.
- Union/map/list_view/run_end_encoded: implement if it is a small addition using the same pattern (map = list of struct; list views need per-row offset+size copy); otherwise leave on the fallback and say so.
- Chunked take: convert global indices to (chunk, local) with a cursor over chunk boundaries (indices are arbitrary, so binary search over prefix sums or a sorted pass), group per chunk, run the flat kernel per chunk, then one N-ary concat of the pieces in output order. Simplest correct approach that hits the target wins; a sort-by-chunk permutation then an inverse permutation is acceptable if it beats concat-first. Filter on chunked: per-chunk dense u32 selections (appendBoolSelections already takes a base), per-chunk take, N-ary concat.
- N-ary nested concat in concat_array_refs.zig: list/large_list = N-ary offsets rebase + ONE recursive concat of the children (children of each part are sliced to the part's row range: use the offsets of each part to compute the child range exactly as the pairwise path does); struct = validity N-ary + per-child recursive concat of the parts' children (row-aligned children sliced to the part window); fixed_size_list = validity + child concat of child slices; dictionary with identical dictionaries (same storage pointer) = concat indices and share the dictionary, else fall back; extension = concat storage and re-wrap. Keep validateLayout on the result as the existing N-ary path does.
- Trust boundaries: these kernels run on already-validated arrays, but indices are caller input: keep checkIndices; any offsets read from arrays must stay bounds-checked (the fuzz compute target exercises take/filter/concat/slice on decoded data and panics on any validateFull failure of the result, so every result must be valid).

## Rules
- Ponytail: minimal diffs, reuse the existing helpers (gatherBits, checkIndices, validityBytes, copyShort, wildCopy, appendValidityBits, binaryDataRange), no new files beyond the two benchmarks, no new abstractions.
- No @backingInt/@fromBackingInt or 0.17-only std APIs. Produce an LF patch; files are CRLF on disk. Bash heredocs with large bodies fail on this machine: write files with the Write tool.
- Toolchains: Zig 0.17 = `zig`; Zig 0.16 = C:\Users\cable\tools\zig-x86_64-windows-0.16.0\zig.exe always with `--cache-dir .zig-cache16`; never run both at once; use -j2 and retry once on the zstd compile flake. Benchmarks: `zig build benchmark-<name>_benchmark -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -j2`, one at a time.
- Tests: for each new kernel one test comparing against the existing per-row path (datumTakeNullable on the same input before your change is the oracle: keep a copy of the old function under a test-only name if needed, or compare against slice+concat results) on an input with nulls, a non-zero offset (sliced input), and a null index; plus the chunked paths. src/compute/test_datum.zig has the existing style.
- Verify: `zig build test -j2` on both compilers (375 + yours), `zig build fuzz-corpus -j2` on both, 0.16 `zig fmt` clean on touched files (tr -d '\r' < f | zig16 fmt --stdin | cmp), `python tools/test_benchmark_ci_check.py`, then `python tools/fuzz.py --optimize ReleaseSafe --out .fuzz-out run --targets compute,array-layout,c-abi --seconds 180` with no findings (fresh .fuzz-out). The compute target panics if any take/filter/concat/slice result fails validateFull or has the wrong length, so it is your correctness oracle too.

content.text:
Round 5 is reviewed, verified and merged. Master is at 15480a1 on Gewelf-Labs/zarrow and pushed.

**What changed**

- string_view and binary_view take gathers the 16-byte view structs and shares the data buffers unchanged.
- dense_union take gathers type ids, builds one index list per child by counting sort and takes each child once. Undeclared type ids and offsets past the child are rejected.
- run_end_encoded take maps each index to its run, merges consecutive rows of one run, and takes the values child once per output run. Outputs longer than the run-end type are rejected.
- Every layout now has a direct take kernel, so the per-row chunked fallback is deleted.

**Before and after** (ns/row, 200k rows, Zig 0.17 ReleaseFast)

| benchmark | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| string_view take | ~195,000 | 3.4-4.9 |
| dense_union take | UnsupportedType | 9.6-10.9 |
| run_end_encoded take | UnsupportedType | 5.5-6.0 |

The other take benchmarks are unchanged within noise. The old view take was quadratic and used about 30 GB on 200k rows, which is why its baseline is so large.

**Verification**: 379 tests pass on both compilers, the fuzz corpus replays clean on both, 0.16 fmt is clean, the benchmark CI checker tests pass, and the Docker Linux campaign ran 6.2M mutation execs plus 1.8M coverage-guided runs with no findings.

Still unsupported: concat for dense_union, run_end_encoded and the view types, so filtering a chunked array of those layouts into a single array still fails as before. That is the one remaining compute gap from the speed review.
continue

input.prompt:
You are implementing performance round 6 for zarrow, a Zig-native Apache Arrow library. Goal: N-ary concat for the layouts still returning UnsupportedType or using the pairwise merge: dense_union, run_end_encoded, string_view, binary_view (plus list_view/large_list_view if it fits the same pattern cheaply). After this, `concatArrayRefs` should handle every Arrow layout zarrow supports, and filtering a chunked dense_union/REE datum into one array should work. Deliver a patch plus notes; do not touch the original worktree.

## Setup
- Source repo (read only for you): C:\Users\cable\Documents\dev\zarrow\.claude\worktrees\zig-0-17-migration-branch-f92e21, HEAD 219c078 (round 5 merged). Work in a short scratch path: create C:\Users\cable\AppData\Local\Temp\fz6 (delete if present), fill with `git -C <repo> archive HEAD | tar -x -C <fz6>`, `git init` + commit inside so you can diff. Make a base copy C:\Users\cable\AppData\Local\Temp\fz6b for A/B. Deep paths break link.exe and git on Windows: stay in those short dirs.
- Zig 0.17 = `zig` on PATH. Zig 0.16 = `C:\Users\cable\tools\zig-x86_64-windows-0.16.0\zig.exe` always with `--cache-dir .zig-cache16`. NEVER run both compilers at once (shared global cache). Always `-j2`; a zstd vendor compile flake happens occasionally, retry once. Code must compile on both: no `@backingInt/@fromBackingInt`, no 0.17-only std APIs. CI lint is 0.16 `zig fmt`. The fz6 tree is LF, keep it LF.
- Bash heredocs with big bodies fail on this machine: use the Write tool for files. Benchmarks: `zig build benchmark-<name>_benchmark -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -j2`, one at a time, machine noisy; alternate base/new runs for A/B (scratchpad ab4.sh is a harness you may copy).
- Scratchpad for deliverables: C:\Users\cable\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-cable-Documents-dev-zarrow--claude-worktrees-zig-0-17-migration-branch-f92e21\3ab19c71-6c26-4cbd-ba49-bd6ba48132fc\scratchpad\ . Read perf4_notes.md and perf5_notes.md there first: they document concatManyFlat / concatManyNested / Part windows / childWindow / concatParts / offsetsRange / rebaseOffsets in src/concat_array_refs.zig, and the take kernels (takeDenseUnionArray, takeRunEnds, takeByteViewArray) in src/compute/datum_permutation.zig whose conventions you should mirror. The per-row oracle test `rowsEqual` in src/compute/test_datum.zig and the test "concatArrayRefs N-ary nested path matches the source rows for sliced parts" are what you extend.

## What to build (src/concat_array_refs.zig)
1. string_view / binary_view N-ary concat: today a pairwise merge through the view builders (concatStringViewArray/concatBinaryViewArray, mergePairs). Replace with one pass: concatenate the view structs (16 B each), concatenate the lists of variadic data buffers (retain, do not copy) and rebase each part's out-of-line views' buffer_index by the number of data buffers preceding that part; inline views (length <= 12) copy as is. Reject a part whose out-of-line view references a buffer index >= its own buffer count or whose offset+length exceeds that buffer (hostile input). Validity via appendValidityBits as the other N-ary paths do. The result must pass validateLayout (call it as the other paths do). Delete the pairwise view merge, mergePairs and concatTwoArrayRefs if nothing else uses them afterwards (check all callers first; `concatArrayRefs` parts.len == 1 path uses concatTwoArrayRefs today: make the single-part case go through the N-ary path too, keeping the "fresh compacted copy, offset 0" contract that the existing tests check).
2. dense_union N-ary concat: concatenate type ids; for each child, concatenate the child windows as whole children (dense union children are not row-aligned, every part contributes its entire child array, or if the part is a slice, still the whole child since offsets index into it: simplest correct approach is to concat whole children and rebase each part's offsets by the running child length per type id). Reject offsets that are negative or >= the part's child length and undeclared type ids. Validate type ids declared lists match across parts (dataTypeEql covers the type). Result through validateLayout.
3. run_end_encoded N-ary concat: for each part, its physical runs are those overlapping [offset, offset+length) (see takeRunEnds / findRun / runEndsWindow in src/array/array_data.zig for the convention: run ends are in the child's coordinate space and must be compared against offset+idx). Output: run ends rebased to the output logical row space (clamp the first run's start to the part's offset and the last run's end to offset+length, then shift by the output row position), values child = concat of the parts' physical value windows (Part windows, through concatParts). Reject run ends not covering the part, non-monotone run ends, and outputs that do not fit the run-end type. Do not merge equal values across part boundaries (not required by the spec).
4. list_view / large_list_view N-ary concat only if it fits the same window pattern cheaply (offsets rebased by the running child length, child windows = whole child since views can point anywhere): otherwise leave it UnsupportedType and say so.
5. Benchmarks: add cases to benchmarks/concat_nested_benchmark.zig (names `concat_nested_string_view`, `concat_nested_dense_union`, `concat_nested_ree`), 12,500 parts × 16 rows like the existing cases, register them in tools/benchmark_ci_check.py EXPECTED_BENCHES, tools/benchmark_ci_thresholds.json and tools/test_benchmark_ci_check.py VALID_ROWS. Targets: < 10 ns/row each.
6. Tests: extend the concat oracle test with these sources (full and sliced parts, an empty part, parts with nulls), validateFull on every result, hostile cases rejected (view buffer index out of range, union offset past child, run ends not covering), and a chunked-datum filter of dense_union and REE through datumFilter now succeeding with array output and matching the flat filter.

## Rules
- ponytail: smallest working code, reuse the Part/childWindow/concatParts machinery, no new abstractions; every path keeps the bounds checks (concat inputs may come from hostile IPC data; the fuzz compute target exercises concat on every decoded column and validateFull on the result). Never loosen validation.
- Verify on the final code: `zig build test -j2` on both compilers, `zig build fuzz-corpus -j2` on both, 0.16 fmt clean on touched files, `python -I tools/test_benchmark_ci_check.py`, and `python tools/fuzz.py --optimize ReleaseSafe --out .fuzz-out run --targets compute,array-layout,c-abi --seconds 180` on fz6 (a `hang | |` with no frames on c-abi is a known load artifact; anything else is a finding to fix; a reproducer goes in fuzz/corpus/<dir>/regress-<8 hex>.bin).
- Deliverables: `<scratchpad>\perf6.patch` (LF, `git apply --check` must pass against a `git archive HEAD` tree of 219c078) and `<scratchpad>\perf6_notes.md` (root causes, design, trust boundaries, tests, verification, before/after table, what was deleted). Final report: 10 lines max plus the table.

Round 6 is reviewed, verified and merged. Master is at 483f974 on Gewelf-Labs/zarrow and pushed.

**What changed**

- Concat is now N-ary for every layout zarrow supports. The pairwise merge, its view builders and the two-array concat helper are deleted.
- string_view and binary_view copy the 16-byte views, share the data buffers and rebase out-of-line buffer indices after checking them against the part's own buffers.
- Dense union concatenates each child's offset window and rebases offsets per type id. Undeclared ids and offsets past the child are rejected.
- Run-end encoded takes the runs overlapping each part, clamps the last run end and shifts run ends to output rows. Non-increasing run ends and outputs too long for the run-end type are rejected.
- Sparse union, list_view and large_list_view ride the same window pass. Filtering a chunked union, run-end-encoded or view datum into one array now works.

**Before and after** (ns/row, 12,500 parts × 16 rows, Zig 0.17 ReleaseFast)

| benchmark | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| string_view concat | ~8,350 | 5.6-6.3 |
| dense_union concat | UnsupportedType | 8.8-9.5 |
| run_end_encoded concat | UnsupportedType | 6.5-6.7 |

List and struct concat and the flat concat control are unchanged within noise.

**Verification**: 380 tests pass on both compilers, the fuzz corpus replays clean on both, 0.16 fmt is clean, the benchmark CI checker tests pass, and the Docker Linux campaign ran 7.0M mutation execs plus 1.8M coverage-guided runs with no findings.

That closes every compute gap the speed review listed; the remaining unmeasured areas from that review are dictionary encoding and the UTF-8 validation cost inside validateFull.

## (A) Concat of dictionary parts with different dictionaries

Before: `concatManyFlat` returned null when the parts did not share one dictionary node and
`concatParts` answered `UnsupportedType` (the last one left). Chunked filters / array-output takes
of dictionary chunks with different dictionaries therefore failed when they concatenated their
per-chunk pieces.

Existing code: there was no dictionary unifier or hash-based dictionary builder in src/
(`DictionaryBuilder` only appends given indices). So the hashing is new, ~200 lines in
`concat_array_refs.zig`.

Design (`concatDictionaries(T)`, dispatched from `concatParts` on the index type, 8 widths/signs):
- Value types: fixed-width (flatKind `.fixed`, width > 0) and string/binary/large (keys are the
  value bytes). bool, null, nested, view and dictionary value types stay `UnsupportedType`.
- Pass 1 over the parts: types (`checkPartType`), rows, may-have-nulls, and every distinct
  dictionary by node (`AutoHashMap(node -> {remap base, len})`; consecutive parts with the same
  node skip the lookup). The values buffer bounds each dictionary length
  (`buffers[1].len / width >= offset + length`) before anything is sized by it.
- Scratch sized once from pass 1: the old->new remap table (sum of distinct dictionary lengths,
  one T each), the key map and the merged offsets/values. Growing them cost more than the hashing
  (Windows hands out fresh pages for every regrown block).
- Pass 2, one pass over the parts: validity bits; on the first part that refers to a dictionary,
  `mergeDictionary` hashes its values once (Wyhash) and fills its remap rows (per value, not per
  row): the first dictionary is appended as is (its duplicates keep their own index, identity
  remap), later ones add only values not seen before, in first-seen order; null entries share one
  null slot (the first null seen). Then the part's indices are gathered through the remap table;
  null rows get index 0.
- Merged values (`MergedValues`): appended bytes (+ end offsets for string/binary, null entry
  positions), built into the output dictionary at the end (`finish`, `validateLayout`). The key
  map holds 4-byte entry numbers hashed through the merged bytes (`EntryContext` /
  `BytesProbe` adapters on `std.HashMapUnmanaged`), so it stays small and lookups never touch
  the input dictionaries again. (A first version kept Part windows and built the merged
  dictionary with `concatParts`; that re-read every dictionary a second time and was slower.)
- The result keeps the requested type; it fails with `InvalidInput` when an entry number exceeds
  `maxInt(T)` (e.g. a 257th value with uint8 indices; no widening), when a non-null index is
  negative or `>= its part's dictionary length`, when a part has no dictionary, or when the merged
  string bytes exceed i32. Result: `validateLayout`.
- Shared-dictionary fast path unchanged (`concatManyFlat`).
- `takeChunked`: random takes still use per-run pieces when the chunks have different
  dictionaries (explicit node check before concat-first, so no unification there); array-output
  callers (filter, takeAsArray) concat the pieces once, which now unifies.

content.text:
Round 7 is merged into master and pushed as d459e0d (worktree commit 20dc3e9).

**What landed**
- Concat of dictionary parts with different dictionaries now produces one merged dictionary instead of failing. Indices are remapped per dictionary value, the index type is never widened, and out-of-range indices, mismatched dictionary value types or overflow are rejected. I added the value-type check during review; the rest of the patch held up at the trust boundaries.
- `validateFull` now checks UTF-8 of non-null string, large_string and string_view values. This is a tightening: arrays with invalid UTF-8 that used to pass now fail. Cost is 0.10 ns/byte.
- A new `dictionaryEncode` kernel, exported from the root module.
- A fuzz-found crash from round 6 is fixed: concat of dense unions with no children indexed an empty window table. Reproducer added to the corpus.

**Verification**
- Tests: 384/384 on Zig 0.17 and 0.16. Corpus replay clean on both. 0.16 fmt clean. CI checker tests pass.
- Docker campaign: 7.2M executions plus 1.8M coverage runs, no findings.

**Benchmarks** (ns/row, 200k rows, ReleaseFast, quiet machine)

| benchmark | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| concat_nested_dictionary | UnsupportedType | 59.8 |
| dictionary_encode_string | no kernel | 15.3 |
| dictionary_encode_int32 | no kernel | 13.5 |
| validate_full_string | 0.50 (no UTF-8 check) | 1.64 |
| validate_full_int32_list (control) | 1.12 | 1.12 |
| flat and nested concat controls | unchanged | unchanged |

The dictionary concat missed its 30 ns target. The benchmark shape is 12,500 separately allocated dictionaries with 100k distinct values; the kernel runs at 14 ns/row when in cache, and the rest is hash-probe cache misses and page faults on fresh scratch. Reusable scratch would need an API change, so I left it.
